title: The geyser that gave every geyser its name now rarely erupts
body: The English word *geyser* comes from **Geysir**, a hot spring in Iceland’s Haukadalur valley whose name comes from the Icelandic verb *geysa*, “to gush”. Geysir can hurl boiling water up to 60 m into the air, but its eruptions are now infrequent, and in the past it has stopped entirely for years at a time. Its moods follow the earthquakes: quakes have repeatedly revived it, and it has then subsided again. Because its neighbour Strokkur erupts every few minutes, photos and videos of Strokkur are regularly mislabelled as Geysir.

cover.alt: A bulging dome of turquoise water rising from a geyser pool on a pale, steaming plain under big clouds

slides.alt: A dome of turquoise water bulges up from a geyser pool, then bursts into a tall white column of boiling water and steam that billows sideways in the wind while onlookers watch from a distance.
slides.caption: Not Geysir but its neighbour Strokkur, in July 2010: a dome of turquoise water bulges up from the pool, then bursts into a column of boiling water and steam.
slides.music: “I Can Feel it Coming” Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com) · CC BY 4.0

slides.label: the year the name Geysir first appears in writing
slides.text: A geyser at the site was already described in a book finished around 1206 by the Danish historian Saxo Grammaticus.

slides.heading: How high the water goes
slides.note: In 2000, after earthquakes, Geysir reached 122 m for two days

slides.heading: Geysir or Strokkur?

items.text: Often passed off as the other in photos

slides.explanation: Geysir is the old, famous and now mostly quiet one; Strokkur is the busy neighbour that most visitors actually see erupt.

slides.question: The hot springs at Geysir are far older than Geysir itself. For roughly how long have they been active?
slides.explanation: Hot springs have been active at the site for roughly 10,000 years, while Geysir itself is thought to have started forming around 1150 CE.
